context_blurb:
Look closely at a meadow or a forest and you will find living things tangled together: a bee in a flower, a tick on a deer, a lynx chasing a hare. Biologists sort these meetings with one simple test: what does each side gain, and what does it lose?

Biologists call it symbiosis when two different species, two kinds of living thing, share their lives closely over a long stretch of time. In everyday talk the word often means a partnership where both sides win, but to a biologist it covers three types. What sorts them is whether each partner is helped, harmed or neither. In mutualism both gain; in commensalism one gains and the other is neither helped nor harmed; in parasitism one partner, the parasite, gains at the cost of the other, its host.

A honeybee visits a flower to drink its nectar, a sweet juice. While it feeds, pollen, the fine dust a flower makes, catches in the hairs on its body. At its next stop some of that dust brushes off, and the carried pollen lets that plant make seeds. The bee gets food and the plant gets its pollen delivered, so both gain: mutualism.

Trillions of bacteria, living things far too small to see, live in your large intestine, the last stretch of your gut. They digest fibre, the tough part of plant food your body cannot break down, and many make vitamins such as vitamin K. In return they get a home and a share of the food.

Pull up a clover or a bean plant and you will find little lumps on its roots, each crowded with bacteria. Air is mostly nitrogen gas, which plants need but cannot use as it is. The bacteria in the lumps take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form the roots can soak up, and the plant pays them with sugar from its leaves.

High in a rainforest, an orchid perches on a branch to reach the light. Its roots grip the bark and drink in rain and mist, and it takes no water or food from inside the tree. The orchid gains a sunny perch, and the tree is neither helped nor harmed: commensalism. Biologists admit it is hard to prove the tree is truly unaffected, since a tiny cost could go unseen.

In parasitism one side pays. A tick fastens onto a deer and feeds on its blood for days, then drops off once it is full. The tick gains a meal and the deer loses blood, and a heavy load of ticks can wear an animal down, so this is parasitism. It is not predation: a predator kills and eats its prey, while a parasite feeds on a host that usually lives on.

A tapeworm hooks onto its host's gut wall and soaks up digested food for years, giving nothing back. Yet a tapeworm rarely kills the person it lives in, because it needs a living host to feed and spread. A host killed quickly would leave the worm no time to send its eggs on to new hosts.

Even a green plant can be a parasite. Mistletoe's leaves catch sunlight and make part of its food, yet a root-like part of it grows into the branch to take water and minerals that the tree carries up from its roots. Unlike the orchid, it gains at the tree's cost, and a heavy load can stunt or kill a tree.

Predation, the fourth way species meet, is not counted as symbiosis at all. For nearly a century, trappers sold lynx furs to the Hudson's Bay Company in Canada, which counted them each year, and hare records cover the same span. Side by side, both counts rise and fall in waves about ten years long. Lynx live mostly on snowshoe hares, so their numbers can climb only after the hares have grown plentiful, and the lynx peaks come a year or two after the hares peak.

Why, then, do the hares never vanish? As hares grow scarce, lynx grow fewer too. With little left to catch, many lynx starve and few of their kittens live, and with fewer hunters about, the last hares breed back up and the cycle begins again. Food for the hares plays a part as well.
